I have farmed this land for 40 years, since I was 14 years old. I never went to school, but I know what works by watching and doing. My family works 42 mu, which is a good-sized piece. I plant 28 mu with wheat and maize — wheat in the winter, then maize right after we cut the wheat in early June. The other land is 10 mu of cotton and 4 mu of cucumber. The cucumber brings the best money per mu when the market price is high.

For wheat, I do the same as last year. After the maize stalks are cleared, I run the rotary tiller and sow an improved wheat variety — the same kind my neighbor Lao Wang used. His wheat stood up well to the wind last year. Each mu gets one 50-jin bag of compound fertilizer spread before sowing. When the wheat turns green in spring, I top-dress with half a bag of urea, about 20 jin per mu. I have done this for many years. It usually gives me about 500 jin per mu. I irrigate three times: once in late winter if the ground is dry, once when the wheat starts jointing, and once when the grain is filling. I spray twice — herbicide right after sowing, and then once more in spring for aphids or rust if it shows up. I thought about cutting back on fertilizer because the price went up, but no. Lao Zhang is using the same amount as last year. Better to waste a little fertilizer than to lose yield. A thin crop is a disaster.

For maize, I plant hybrid seed with the no-till seeder straight into the wheat stubble the same week we harvest. No point plowing — that wastes diesel and time, and the stubble keeps some moisture. Each mu gets one bag of compound fertilizer at planting. When the plants are waist-high, at the big trumpet stage, I spread half a bag of urea. I irrigate twice: once when the stalks are shooting up, and once when the ears are filling. Two sprays — one for weeds, and one for corn borer if the worms come.

Cotton is on 10 mu. I plough that land deep because cotton roots need loose soil. I plant improved cotton seed. Each mu gets one bag of compound fertilizer at planting, and half a bag of urea when the flowers open. Cotton needs potash or the bolls turn yellow and don't open right, so I add about 30 jin of potassium fertilizer per mu. I learned that from my cousin — his cotton looked bad until he started adding potash. I irrigate three times: when the seedlings are small, at flowering, and when the bolls are swelling. Cotton needs five sprays. The bollworms and aphids never stop.

The cucumber is only 4 mu but it is hard work. I till it with the rotary tiller. I plant hybrid cucumber seeds — the kind that give long, straight fruits that the buyers like. Before planting I spread two cartloads of rotted chicken manure on each mu. Then I put down one and a half bags of compound fertilizer and one full bag of urea per mu. Cucumber eats more than grain crops. I water six times, more if the heat comes early. I spray five times for downy mildew and whiteflies.

That is my plan. Last year was decent — not the best, but decent. The grain prices were stable and cucumber paid well. So I will not change much. I have the well for water, though diesel for the pump is expensive. I have to watch the total cost. But fertilizer is not where I save money. If the neighbors are doing the same, I feel safe.
